workingTitle: One solar eruption squeezed another into a stronger storm
publicationStatus: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters; arXiv version submitted November 13, 2026
coreFacts: Three homologous coronal mass ejections left solar active region 13664 within one day on May 8, 2024, before the severe May 10 geomagnetic storm.
The study combined remote observations from SUTRI, SDO, SOHO, and STEREO-A with near-Earth Wind measurements and a three-dimensional solar-wind simulation.
The simulation compared two interacting-CME cases with a control containing only the first eruption.
In the interaction cases, the later eruption compressed the first one and limited its expansion, maintaining a stronger magnetic field as the combined structure traveled toward Earth.
The modeled southward magnetic-field component near Earth exceeded 60 nanoteslas in the interaction cases, about twice the roughly 30 nanoteslas in the single-CME control.
A southward interplanetary magnetic field couples efficiently to Earth's magnetic field, so preserving that component can intensify a geomagnetic storm.

sources.label: Wang et al., accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters

sourceStatus: Full accepted manuscript, abstract, methods, controlled simulation cases, numerical results, and limitations read; measured observations and model-based interpretation checked separately.
caveats: The compression mechanism is inferred from a physics-based simulation constrained by observations, not directly measured throughout the journey from the Sun to Earth.
The event-matching simulation reached Earth about 11 hours earlier than the actual disturbance.
The study analyzes one event and varies only the magnetic helicity of the second eruption; separation, speed, direction, and topology remain to be tested systematically.
Assigning individual CME intervals near Earth is partly model-dependent because the merged structure was complex.
